A federal appeals court ruled two to one against the administration last week, with the dissenting judge arguing the challengers didn't even have standing to sue in the first place. The White House says it plans to take the case to the Supreme Court, though as of this morning that appeal hasn't actually been filed. The lower court's hold on construction runs out around August twenty first, so that's the clock everyone's watching.

ANDREW: A couple of other things worth flagging quickly. The administration's new vaccine schedule executive order, signed Monday, cuts the recommended childhood vaccine list from eighteen diseases to eleven and splits the MMR shot into three separate visits. Major doctors' groups, including the American Medical Association, are pushing back hard, though no lawsuit has been filed against this specific order yet. And in Congress, the House and Senate are still stuck on dueling short term funding bills, one running to December fourth, the other to December eleventh. Lawmakers are on recess until September, with a government shutdown deadline looming September thirtieth.

ANDREW: Let's follow that inflation number over to where it hits home most directly, mortgage rates.

ANDREW: The thirty year fixed rate eased after yesterday's report, now sitting around six point six percent according to Mortgage News Daily, its lowest point in a few weeks. Freddie Mac's more conservative weekly survey still has it a touch higher, at six point six nine percent, but the direction is the same either way: down.

JENNY: Is that actually enough to get buyers off the sidelines?

ANDREW: A little. The Mortgage Bankers Association says applications rose three point six percent last week. Purchase applications were up three percent, and refinancing jumped five percent, though refi activity is still running well below where it was a year ago. It's not a flood, but it's a real shift after a slow summer.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the CFPB is expected to finalize new mortgage servicing rules as soon as this month, aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders under an executive order the administration signed earlier this year. Separately, federal housing regulators are adding a new disclosure requiring lenders to show veterans a side by side cost comparison between FHA and VA loans.

JENNY: Small print, but it could save veterans real money.

ANDREW: Exactly the kind of thing that's easy to miss and expensive to skip.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's get you into Jacksonville. I know the city's got a big day downtown too.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is bracing for a scorcher today, a high near ninety four, feeling more like the upper hundreds. A heat advisory runs from eleven this morning until eight tonight, and there's a decent chance of afternoon thunderstorms on top of it.

JENNY: Down at City Hall, the council's Finance Committee holds its sixth hearing today on Mayor Deegan's two point oh three billion dollar budget, a nine to five session going through the details line by line. The headline is that it doesn't raise the property tax rate at all.

ANDREW: How do you fund a two billion dollar budget without touching the rate?

JENNY: Rising property values and new construction are doing the work. The city says it won't need to dip into reserves for a second straight year, and public safety, JSO and Fire Rescue combined, gets just over one billion dollars. There's also five hundred eighty six million dollars earmarked for capital projects in year one alone. Mayor Deegan is also holding a town hall tonight at Julia Landon College Prep, one stop on an eight city swing to walk residents through the numbers before the council votes in late September.

JENNY: The other story to watch locally: tomorrow's hearing in the special election fight over City Council candidate Deborah Wesley. According to Florida Politics, a circuit judge has set a hearing for Friday at noon on a residency challenge, with a former opponent arguing Wesley didn't actually live in the district long enough to qualify. Her campaign calls it baseless, noting similar challenges were already tossed out twice this cycle. The election itself is Monday, August eighteenth, and if nobody clears fifty percent among the three candidates, it goes to a runoff in November.

ANDREW: Five days out and still fighting over who's even on the ballot.

JENNY: That's Jacksonville politics for you this summer.

JENNY: And a quick note for football fans. The city's moving ahead with a two point one two million dollar temporary seating plan at EverBank Stadium, adding club level risers to make up for construction areas that are offline. Capacity this season is down to about forty two thousand five hundred, roughly sixty two percent of normal, while the Stadium of the Future renovation is underway. The preseason opener against Carolina is August twenty first, with a second preseason game against Tampa Bay a week later, and organizers say the project is actually running ahead of schedule.

ANDREW: Good to hear something's ahead of schedule this year.

JENNY: I'll take good news wherever I can get it these days.

JENNY: Let's jump from budget hearings to boardrooms, because there's been a wild couple of days in AI.

JENNY: Bloomberg reported this morning that Anthropic is in talks to acquire an Israeli startup called Decart for something in the neighborhood of six billion dollars. Neither company has confirmed it, and the deal isn't done.

ANDREW: What does Decart actually make that's worth that kind of money?

JENNY: Real time video generation and simulation tools, technology that could let AI systems interact with realistic virtual environments as they're being created, rather than rendering them frame by frame afterward. It was founded by veterans of an Israeli military intelligence unit and was valued at around four billion dollars just this past May.

JENNY: That's not even the biggest number floating around Anthropic this week. Separate reporting out of the Financial Times suggests the company could pursue an IPO as early as October, at a valuation approaching two trillion dollars, which would make it the largest public offering in history, bigger than SpaceX. Again, Anthropic hasn't confirmed any of this publicly.

ANDREW: Two trillion is a number that's hard to even picture for a company that's only a few years old.

JENNY: It is. Treat it as very much a rumor for now, not a plan.

JENNY: Meanwhile, over at OpenAI, longtime chief operating officer Brad Lightcap is leaving after nine years, the latest in a string of senior departures that's included former president Fidji Simo just last month. OpenAI says he's leaving to start something new.

ANDREW: That's a lot of turnover at the top of a company moving this fast.

JENNY: It is. Worth watching whether it slows anything down on the product side.

JENNY: One more from the AI world. Google is restructuring its DeepMind division after Demis Hassabis stepped down as CEO last week to become chairman and chief scientist. Koray Kavukcuoglu now runs DeepMind day to day, reporting directly to Sundar Pichai, and Google is folding several other AI teams into the division. Alphabet shares dropped about four percent on the news, and reports point to internal friction, including missed deadlines and a wave of departures.

ANDREW: Any names we'd recognize among those departures?

JENNY: The biggest one: Jeff Dean, one of Google's most senior AI researchers, left the company entirely to start his own venture.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this weekend: Saturday, August sixteenth. That's when the sixty day toll free shipping window through the Strait of Hormuz expires. If Iran and the US can't agree on a longer deal before then, watch oil prices first, and mortgage rates soon after. That's the direct line from geopolitics to your monthly payment right now.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
